reason: The sources provide multi-site documentation of Sagan's life, scientific work, TV career, and the origin of his famous catchphrase misquote.
story: Carl Sagan was one of the most famous science communicators in history. Born in New York City in 1934, he earned his degrees from the University of Chicago and went on to teach at Harvard and Cornell. As a planetary scientist, Sagan correctly predicted the scorching surface temperature of Venus caused by a runaway greenhouse effect and contributed to NASA missions like Mariner 2 and Voyager 1. He even suggested taking the legendary Pale Blue Dot photograph of Earth from four billion miles away. Sagan co-wrote and hosted the 13-part 1980 television series Cosmos, which reached over 500 million viewers worldwide. Though popular culture forever linked him to the catchphrase billions and billions thanks to Johnny Carson's Tonight Show impressions, Sagan actually used terms like billions upon billions to stress the hard consonant b. Sagan spent his life inspiring global audiences to study the universe before passing away in 1996.
angle: Carl Sagan became globally famous for the catchphrase 'billions and billions', yet comedian Johnny Carson actually popularized the phrase while parodying Sagan's distinct delivery on television.

claims.claim: Carl Sagan was born in New York City on November 9, 1934.
Sagan earned four academic degrees from the University of Chicago, concluding with a doctorate in 1960.
Sagan taught and conducted astronomical research at Harvard University early in his career.
Sagan served as a professor at Cornell University and directed its Laboratory for Planetary Studies.
Sagan assisted NASA in designing and managing the Mariner 2 mission to Venus.
Sagan correctly predicted that Venus maintained an extremely hot surface temperature driven by a runaway greenhouse effect.
Sagan served as a key scientist on NASA's Voyager program exploring the outer planets.
Sagan proposed turning Voyager 1's camera around to photograph Earth, producing the famous Pale Blue Dot photo.
Sagan co-founded The Planetary Society to promote space exploration.
Sagan co-wrote and hosted the 13-part public television documentary series Cosmos: A Personal Voyage.
The Cosmos documentary series was watched by over 500 million people across 60 countries.
Johnny Carson parodied Sagan on The Tonight Show for his emphasized pronunciation of the word billions.
Sagan authored hundreds of scientific papers and popular science works during his lifetime.
Sagan was a pioneer in exobiology, researching the possibility of extraterrestrial life.
Sagan died at age 62 in December 1996 from pneumonia following a battle with myelodysplasia.
